WHY WARM WATER TURNS CORAL REEFS WHITE

Coral reefs along parts of Taiwan's southern coast, including areas near Kenting, have experienced repeated bleaching events over the past decade, a phenomenon that alarms marine biologists studying the region's underwater ecosystems.

Coral bleaching occurs when ocean temperatures rise even slightly above a coral's normal tolerance range, often by just one or two degrees Celsius sustained over several weeks. Under stress, coral expels the colourful algae living inside its tissue, algae that normally provide the coral with both its vibrant colour and most of its food energy through photosynthesis. Without these algae, the coral turns pale white and becomes far more vulnerable to disease and starvation.

Bleaching does not always mean death. If water temperatures drop back to normal relatively quickly, coral can sometimes recover and rebuild its relationship with algae over several months. However, repeated bleaching events, occurring more frequently as ocean temperatures continue rising globally, leave coral increasingly little time to recover between episodes.

Researchers at a marine station near Kenting have begun testing whether selectively breeding coral that survived previous bleaching events could produce offspring more resistant to heat stress. Early results are promising but preliminary, and scientists caution that breeding heat-resistant coral cannot substitute for addressing the underlying cause: rising ocean temperatures driven by global climate change.

Local dive operators, who depend economically on healthy reefs, have started participating in citizen science programs, reporting bleaching observations that help researchers track the problem across a wider area than research teams alone could cover.
stem: According to the passage, what does coral expel from its tissue when it is under heat stress?
options: The colourful algae that normally provide colour and food energy
Small fish that typically live and hide within coral structures
Excess salt water that has built up inside its structure
Bacteria that cause disease in stressed coral reefs
explain_zh: 文中明確提到珊瑚受壓力時會「expels the colourful algae living inside its tissue」，這些藻類提供珊瑚色彩與大部分食物能量，故選A。B、C、D 文章都沒有提到，屬於捏造的細節。細節題直接對照原文敘述即可判斷。

INTERVIEW: LIFE AS A LICENSED STREET PERFORMER IN TAIPEI

Reporter: You've been performing as a street violinist in Ximending for six years now. How did you get started?

A-Ting: I actually started almost by accident. I was practising in a park one evening, and a small crowd gathered and started leaving coins in my violin case. I hadn't even set it out intentionally. That night made me realise there might be a real audience for this.

Reporter: Taipei requires performers to apply for a license and audition for a specific spot. Was that process difficult?

A-Ting: It was more competitive than I expected. Hundreds of performers apply for a limited number of approved locations each year, and you're judged on a short live audition. Getting a spot in a busy area like Ximending means my income is fairly steady, but performers who get less popular locations often struggle to make performing pay enough on its own.

Reporter: What's the hardest part of this job that people might not expect?

A-Ting: Honestly, it's the unpredictability. Weather ruins an entire evening's earnings instantly, and some nights almost no one stops no matter how well I play. There's also no sick leave, no guaranteed pay. If I don't perform, I don't earn anything that day.

Reporter: Despite that, you've stayed with it for six years. Why?

A-Ting: There's something honest about street performing. People stop, listen, and pay only if they genuinely want to. That direct connection with an audience is something I never found doing anything else.
stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the interview?
options: Street performing in Taipei requires no license and anyone can perform anywhere
A-Ting has decided to quit street performing because the income is too unstable
Despite real challenges like unpredictable income, A-Ting values the direct connection with audiences that street performing offers
Weather has no effect on how much money street performers earn each night
explain_zh: 訪談中阿廷說明表演證申請的競爭、收入的不穩定，卻也強調這份工作與觀眾之間直接的連結讓他堅持六年，C 最能涵蓋全文重點。A、D 與文章內容相反；B 與文章相反（他仍持續表演）。主旨題要抓住受訪者對這份工作整體的評價。

THE MAN WHO SAVED THIRTY THOUSAND SECONDHAND BOOKS

When Chou Ping-an inherited a small bookstore from his father in 2010, most people assumed he would close it within a few years. Physical bookstores across Taiwan were struggling against online retailers and falling reading rates, and secondhand bookstores in particular seemed to belong to an earlier era.

Chou had other plans. Rather than compete directly with large bookstore chains on new releases, he decided to specialise entirely in secondhand books, building relationships with retiring professors, closing libraries, and families clearing out relatives' homes after they passed away. Within a decade, his small shop had grown into a labyrinth of shelves holding more than thirty thousand secondhand volumes, organised by an idiosyncratic system that regular customers eventually learned to navigate.

The turning point came when Chou began posting short videos online describing unusual finds in his collection: a first edition novel with the original owner's handwritten notes in the margins, or a textbook signed by a now-famous scientist decades before their career began. The videos attracted an unexpected following among younger readers who had never previously visited a secondhand bookstore.

Chou insists his goal was never really about business growth. "Every secondhand book has already survived one journey," he says. "My job is just to make sure it gets a second one, instead of ending up thrown away." Today, his shop hosts monthly reading events, and several university students have taken part-time jobs there specifically to learn from his knowledge of rare editions.

options: Chou Ping-an transformed a struggling inherited bookstore into a thriving secondhand book destination
Chou Ping-an closed his father's bookstore shortly after inheriting it in 2010
Large bookstore chains have completely stopped selling any secondhand books
Chou Ping-an's videos have failed to attract any new customers to his shop
explain_zh: 文章描述周先生如何把父親留下的舊書店轉型為專營二手書、吸引年輕讀者的成功書店，A 最能涵蓋全文重點。B、C、D 都與文章內容相反。主旨題要抓住人物傳記中人物做出的關鍵決定與成果。

MAPPING THE OCEAN'S LAST UNCHARTED FRONTIER

More than eighty percent of the world's ocean floor remains unmapped in any detailed way, a striking gap in scientific knowledge given how thoroughly humans have charted the surface of the Moon and Mars. Deep-sea exploration faces unique obstacles that space missions do not: crushing water pressure, complete darkness beyond a few hundred metres, and the sheer scale of the ocean floor, which covers roughly seventy percent of the planet's surface.

Recent advances in autonomous underwater vehicles have begun to close this gap. Unlike earlier research submarines, which required a ship and crew to remain on the surface throughout a dive, modern robotic vehicles can operate independently for days at a time, following pre-programmed routes and surfacing periodically to transmit collected data.

These vehicles have already revealed features previously unknown to science, including underwater mountain ranges taller than anything on land and thriving ecosystems clustered around hydrothermal vents, where chemical-rich water heated by volcanic activity supports life entirely independent of sunlight.

Beyond scientific curiosity, detailed ocean floor maps carry practical importance. They help researchers predict tsunami behaviour more accurately, since underwater terrain significantly affects how waves travel and where they strike land with the greatest force. Mining companies interested in deep-sea mineral deposits also rely on these maps, a use that has drawn criticism from environmental groups concerned about disturbing ecosystems that scientists have barely begun to understand.

Full mapping of the ocean floor at high resolution remains decades away at current progress, according to most estimates from major oceanographic institutions.

WILL AI TRANSLATION MAKE LEARNING A SECOND LANGUAGE POINTLESS?

Real-time AI translation tools have advanced dramatically in recent years, capable of translating spoken conversation almost instantly through earbuds or smartphone apps. Some students, faced with the enormous time investment required to reach fluency in a second language, have begun asking a genuinely provocative question: if a device in my pocket can translate for me, why spend years studying grammar and vocabulary?

Proponents of relying on AI translation point to its practical value. For basic travel, simple business transactions, and everyday communication, current tools already perform well enough to be genuinely useful, and the technology continues improving each year. Time spent memorising vocabulary lists, they argue, might be better invested in other skills.

Language educators, unsurprisingly, push back against this framing. They argue that translation, however accurate, cannot replicate the deeper benefits of language learning, including improved cognitive flexibility, a more intuitive understanding of another culture's assumptions, and the ability to build genuine relationships without a device mediating every exchange. Several studies suggest that people who speak multiple languages show measurable cognitive advantages unrelated to translation ability at all, such as improved multitasking and delayed onset of certain age-related cognitive declines.

There is also a practical limitation critics highlight: AI translation still struggles with humour, idiom, and the subtle emotional tone that fluent speakers convey naturally, meaning something is often lost even when the literal words are translated correctly.

Most linguists conclude that AI translation is a powerful tool but not a genuine substitute for the deeper human experience of learning another language.

FROM COLONIAL EXPORT TO ARTISAN CRAFT: THE STORY OF TAIWANESE TEA

Tea cultivation in the hills around present-day Pinglin and Maokong began in earnest during the nineteenth century, when Taiwanese oolong tea found eager buyers in markets as far away as New York, carried there by merchant ships that made Taiwan's tea trade one of the island's most profitable industries of that era. For decades, tea was grown, processed, and exported almost entirely as a bulk commodity, valued for consistent quantity rather than individual character.

The industry's fortunes shifted dramatically through the twentieth century. Rising labour costs made large-scale bulk export increasingly difficult to sustain profitably, and by the 1970s and 1980s, cheaper tea grown in other countries had captured much of the international bulk market that Taiwanese growers had once dominated.

Rather than disappear, Taiwan's tea industry transformed. Growers who once competed on volume began competing on quality and craftsmanship instead, developing distinctive high-mountain oolong varieties grown at increasingly higher elevations, where cooler temperatures and slower growth produced more complex flavour. Small family farms that survived the bulk-export collapse became specialists, some selling their entire annual harvest to loyal customers who returned year after year for a specific farm's distinctive character.

Today, Taiwanese tea occupies a position almost opposite to its colonial-era origins: rather than competing on low price for mass export, it commands premium prices precisely because of its limited scale and individual character, a transformation few industries manage to complete without simply disappearing along the way.

THE SKY YOU CAN NO LONGER SEE

Residents of major Taiwanese cities who travel to remote mountain areas at night often report the same startling reaction: astonishment at how many stars are visible far from urban centres, a sight increasingly unfamiliar to people who have spent their entire lives under artificially lit skies.

Light pollution, the excessive or misdirected artificial light that brightens night skies over populated areas, has increased steadily worldwide as cities expand and outdoor lighting becomes cheaper and more widespread. Unlike air or water pollution, light pollution leaves no visible residue and causes no immediately obvious health symptoms, which researchers suggest partly explains why it receives comparatively little public attention despite mounting evidence of its effects.

Astronomers were among the first to raise concerns, since observatories increasingly struggle to conduct certain types of research from locations that were reasonably dark just decades ago. More recently, researchers studying human health and wildlife behaviour have documented additional consequences. Excessive nighttime light exposure has been linked to disrupted sleep patterns in humans, while migratory birds, which navigate partly using natural light cues, sometimes become disoriented by bright urban lighting and collide with illuminated buildings during migration season.

Some cities have begun addressing the problem through relatively simple measures: shielded streetlights that direct light downward rather than outward, motion-activated lighting in areas with limited foot traffic at night, and designated "dark sky" zones where lighting is deliberately restricted. Early results from cities that have adopted these measures suggest meaningful improvement in night sky visibility is achievable without compromising public safety.

THE UNCOMFORTABLE QUESTIONS BEHIND VOLUNTEER TOURISM

Every year, thousands of young Taiwanese travellers sign up for short-term volunteer trips abroad, often to build classrooms, teach English, or work briefly at orphanages in developing countries. These trips are typically marketed as mutually beneficial: travellers gain meaningful cultural experience while local communities receive needed help. Increasingly, however, researchers and development workers are asking harder questions about who actually benefits most from these arrangements.

A frequently cited concern involves skill mismatch. Volunteers who spend one or two weeks helping construct a building often possess less relevant construction skill than local workers who could have been paid to do the same job, potentially at lower overall cost and higher quality. Some critics argue that volunteer labour, however well-intentioned, occasionally displaces paid local employment rather than supplementing it.

Orphanage volunteering raises particularly serious concerns. Child welfare researchers have documented cases where children experience repeated emotional attachment and separation as a constant rotation of short-term volunteers comes and goes, a pattern potentially harmful to child development regardless of volunteers' good intentions. Some researchers go further, noting that the presence of paying foreign volunteers has, in certain documented cases, created financial incentive for facilities to keep children in orphanages even when family reunification would have been possible.

None of this means volunteer tourism is inherently harmful. Organisations that involve long-term commitments, genuinely needed skills, and close partnership with local communities can produce real benefit. The uncomfortable lesson is that good intentions alone do not guarantee good outcomes, and prospective volunteers should research an organisation's practices carefully before signing up.
